extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle/Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for understanding, evaluating, and cultivating moral virtue according to Aristotle: virtues are states formed by habit, lie as means between excess and defect, and are judged by practical wisdom with reference to pleasures and pains and voluntary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits formed by repeated acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits are produced from the acts of working like to them; therefore to form virtues we must give a certain character to particular acts because the habits formed correspond to the differences of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises practice from childhood and repeated behavior: what we do repeatedly shapes our character (e.g., accustoming oneself to despise fear produces courage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical aim: not mere speculation but becoming virtuous
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the present treatise is not mere speculation ... we are enquiring not merely that we may know what virtue is but that we may become virtuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral theory must lead to actionable guidance about how to perform particular actions so as to form right habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act in accordance with Right Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We are to act in accordance with Right Reason (a general maxim to be developed later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right Reason will determine the relation between virtues and other faculties; treat moral action as governed by rational judgment rather than rigid rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral deliberation is inexact and context-sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters of moral action and expediency have no fixedness any more than matters of health ... in application to particular cases exactness is not attainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave particulars to agents to judge in context (like a physician or navigator); expect outline principles rather than mechanical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue spoiled by excess and defect; preserved by the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the nature of such things to be spoiled by defect and excess ... the habits of perfected Self-Mastery and Courage are spoiled by the excess and defect, but by the mean state are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the analogy of health: too much or too little training corrupts; aim for the intermediate amount appropriate to the individual and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation and reinforcement of virtues (practice and feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only do we by abstaining from pleasures come to be perfected in Self-Mastery, but when we have come to be so we can best abstain from them ... it is by accustoming ourselves to despise objects of fear and stand up against them that we come to be brave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtues both arise from and make easier the corresponding actions; habits are self-reinforcing. Train by acting rightly and seek outcomes (pleasure/pain) as tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of genuine virtue: pleasure or pain that follows acts
rubrics_metrics.description: For a test of the formation of the habits we must take the pleasure or pain which succeeds the acts; for he is perfected in Self-Mastery who not only abstains ... but is glad to do so; he again is brave who stands up against danger, either with positive pleasure or at least without any pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the agent experiences right pleasure (or absence of pain) in doing the right act — mere compliance without the right feeling is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue's object-matter: pleasures and pains
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Virtue has for its object-matter pleasures and pains, because by reason of pleasure we do what is bad, and by reason of pain decline doing what is right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue theory must focus on correct responses to pleasure and pain; education should train proper pleasurable/painful reactions to objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue defined as habit related to pleasures and pains producing best results
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue then is assumed to be that habit which is such, in relation to pleasures and pains, as to effect the best results, and Vice the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure virtues by their contribution to achieving the best outcomes in relation to pleasures and pains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three primary motives to choice and avoidance (honour, expedient, pleasant)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are principally three things moving us to choice and three to avoidance, the honourable, the expedient, the pleasant; and their three contraries ... the good man is apt to go right, and the bad man wrong, with respect to all these of course, but most specially with respect to pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions consider these three motivators and especially pleasures as commonly misleading; train people to receive pleasure/pain from proper objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of virtue requires knowledge, deliberate preference, and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who do virtuous acts are not in possession of the virtues merely by doing the acts, but must do them 'grammarians-wise' — knowing what they are doing, with deliberate preference for the things’ own sake, and being stable and unapt to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To attribute virtue to an agent require (1) understanding, (2) chosen for its own sake, and (3) a stable disposition — mere right acts by chance or external prompting do not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues are States, not Feelings or Capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings neither the virtues nor vices are ... Capacities we have by nature ... Since then the virtues are neither Feelings nor Capacities, it remains that they must be States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptually locate virtues as dispositional states that regulate feelings and capacities, responsible for praise/blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as a relative mean determined by reason and practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue then is 'a state apt to exercise deliberate choice, being in the relative mean, determined by reason, and as the man of practical wisdom would determine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right mean is relative to the person and circumstances and must be determined by phronesis (practical wisdom); do not seek an absolute arithmetic midpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between absolute mean and mean relative to ourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: By the mean of the thing, i.e. absolute mean, I denote that which is equidistant from either extreme ... But the mean relatively to ourselves must not be so found ... the mean relatively to ourselves must be neither too much nor too little for the particular individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the appropriate mean with regard to the individual's capacities and situation (e.g., Milo vs a novice); tailor moral aims to persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some actions are intrinsically wrong and admit no mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Some there are which are so named as immediately to convey the notion of badness, as malevolence, shamelessness, envy; or, to instance in actions, adultery, theft, homicide; for all these and suchlike are blamed because they are in themselves bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize categories of actions where no intermediate 'mean' can render them right; these are always wrong regardless of proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the mean to particular virtues (schema of examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scheme listing specific spheres where mean state is praiseworthy and extremes blameworthy (examples include Courage for fears and confidence; perfected Self-Mastery for pleasures and pains; Liberality vs Prodigality vs Stinginess; Munificence; Greatness of Soul; Meekness vs Passionateness; Truthfulness; Easy-pleasantry vs Buffoonery; Friendliness vs Complaisance/Flattery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this inventory as worked examples of the golden-mean doctrine; when evaluating character, map behavior to these categories to see whether agent hits the mean or errs toward excess/defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective-relative appraisal: extremes and mean look different from each side
rubrics_metrics.description: The brave man, for instance, shows as rash when compared with the coward, and cowardly when compared with the rash ... the extremes push ... the man in the mean state; the brave man is called a rash man by the coward, and a coward by the rash man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging others, account for comparative viewpoint: what looks like deficiency from one angle may look excessive from another.

rubrics_metrics.name: When exact mean is hard, avoid the extreme more contrary to the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Since to hit exactly on the mean is difficult, one must take the least of the evils as the safest plan ... keep away from that extreme which is more contrary than the other to the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical heuristic: when uncertain, move away from the extreme that is more opposed to the right mean (consider personal bias to identify which extreme is more contrary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion vs voluntariness: external origination determines compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: An action is properly speaking compulsory, when the origination is external to the agent, being such that in it the agent contributes nothing ... that seems to be compulsory 'whose origination is from without, the party compelled contributing nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For assigning praise/blame, classify actions as involuntary if externally compelled and the agent contributed nothing; consider edge cases separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed cases (choice under threat) are 'most like voluntary' and judged accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done from fear of greater evils or to secure others’ safety (ordered by a despot who has your family in his power, or throwing goods overboard in a storm) are of a mixed kind, but are most like voluntary actions because origination rests with the agent at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such cases as choice-worthy at the time and assess praise/blame in light of the occasion and motives rather than absolutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance distinguishes involuntary and 'not-voluntary' actions by remorse
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action of which ignorance is the cause is not-voluntary, but that only is involuntary which is attended with pain and remorse; he who acts by reason of ignorance but is not annoyed at his own action cannot be said to have done it 'with his will' nor 'against' his will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excuse may be given when ignorance of particulars leads to remorseful action; mere ignorance without regret (not-voluntary) is treated differently and may attract blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ignorance of particulars vs ignorance of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance which affects moral choice constitutes depravity but not involuntariness: nor does any ignorance of principle (because for this men are blamed) but ignorance in particular details ... in these there is both compassion and allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excuse is appropriate for ignorance about the concrete particulars of an action (who, what, instrument, result, how) but not for ignorance of moral principles or one’s true interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars that may excuse actions done in ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the particulars: who acts, what he is doing, with respect to what or in what, sometimes with what instrument, and with what result, as that of preservation, and how, as whether softly or violently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing responsibility, inquire into whether the agent was ignorant of these specific facts; ignorance of such particulars can render an action involuntary (if accompanied by remorse).
